paragraphs.text: Deserts cover more than one third of the Earth's land surface, but only quite a small proportion of desert area is sandy – the rest is bare rock or rock fragments. As well as hot deserts, such as the Sahara and Kalahari in Africa, there are also temperate and cold deserts, of which many, such as the Gobi in Asia, owe their origin to being many thousands of kilometres from the oceans, so the rain-bearing winds never reach them.

Deserts receive small and irregular amounts of rainfall, usually less than 250mm per year. However, of greater importance than the amount of rainfall is the effectiveness of the moisture. If a desert receives 100mm of rainfall per year in only two heavy storms, then the effectiveness of the moisture is less than if the rain falls on 20 occasions as a fine drizzle of 5mm. Temperature is also important: when it exceeds 20°C, evaporation rates become very high.

Each year some 120,000 square kilometres of new desert is formed by a process called desertification. This is due to over-cultivation, deforestation, over-grazing and poor irrigation. Desertification occurred in the southern fringes of the Sahara in the 1970s and 1980s.

Deserts are extreme and infertile environments where few species of plants and animals are able to survive. However, this means that competition between desert species is reduced, and for some, life in such an environment is actually easier than fighting for survival in environments where basic resources are plentiful.

The vegetation in all deserts shows extreme adaptation to suit the dry conditions. Smallness of size, leaves reduced to thin spines, long, deep roots, and the ability to grow very quickly at the start of rains are some of the most useful adaptations. The seeds of many desert plants can remain inactive for up to five years, awaiting the occurrence of damp conditions suitable for growth. Other species have adapted to the long, dry spells by storing water in enlarged, fat stems. These are the so-called succulent plants, of which the cacti of the Americas are the best-known examples. The most spectacular cactus is the barrel cactus, which was traditionally used as a water reserve by the Native Americans. Elsewhere in the world, the Euphorbia group of plants predominates in deserts. The stems of these plants are filled with a sticky substance which resists evaporation.

Animal life in deserts is surprisingly varied. Most animals that inhabit them are active primarily at night, or during the brief periods of early morning and late afternoon, when the heat is not as strong. During the day they remain in cooler underground burrows, or in the shade of overhanging rocks. Rodents, snakes, lizards, spiders and insects are the main animal types. There are a few larger animals and birds too.

Many desert animals show strange adaptations for life in these extreme conditions. For example, neither the Saharan jerboa (a tiny rodent) nor the American kangaroo rat appear to drink any water, but instead obtain their moisture directly from their food.

Common characteristics of desert animals are large skin flaps (particularly large ears) from which heat can be lost, an absence of sweat glands, and an ability to lose a large proportion of body weight in the dry season.

One animal which is especially well adapted to life in desert conditions is the camel. Each foot has two toes which are joined by a wide piece of skin that can be spread out, which prevents the animals from sinking into soft sand. The eyes are protected from sand by heavy lashes, while the nostrils can be closed to exclude sand when the animal breathes in. The fatty humps on their back act as food reserves in case of shortage.

The camel's well-known ability to go for long periods without drinking – for over a week while travelling long distances – is due to a number of adaptations designed to save water. Camels do not start to sweat until the temperature reaches 40°C; heat accumulated in the body during the day is given off in the cool of the night. Camels can survive a water loss of about 40% of their body weight without suffering damage, and the water content of the urine is minimised by the kidneys. Following a prolonged period without water, camels have been known to drink over 100 litres in a matter of minutes.

The camel plays a major role in the life of nomadic societies living in the desert, such as the Touareg of north Africa. At the start of the seventh century, Arabs started moving into the coastal regions of Africa, pushing the Touareg into the Sahara Desert. Here the Touareg took on the role of trans-Saharan camel traders, travelling across the desert plains from one destination to the next, and setting up tents along the way. They once travelled the desert in great numbers, but they have now been reduced to small groups. Today, the Touareg are still known for camel trading, but are also involved in rearing cattle and producing metal work. Their crafted swords, jewellery and leather work have become sought-after items in other parts of the world. In addition, traditional Touareg music is now played at international festivals. In these ways, people have become much more aware of these desert nomads and their way of life.
